summary:
Petrova Line is an installable web app that shows how NASA–ISRO’s NISAR radar sees a planet in motion. A scroll-driven 3D story follows NISAR on its 747 km orbit, sends its two radar waves (L-band 24 cm, S-band 9.4 cm) to the ground, builds up its global coverage and visits four places where Earth is changing: a retreating Caspian shore, a flooded Pantanal, the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquake and the Jakobshavn glacier. A radar console then lets anyone compare two dates, switch polarisation and band, read an interferogram, see which scattering mechanism dominates a pixel, and export a short brief.

We answer the challenge by making radar physics (roughness, moisture, structure and phase) visible and hands-on, so people can learn to read SAR images before working with real NISAR data. The scenes are simulated from NISAR’s published parameters and labelled as such.

It matters because radar sees through cloud, smoke and darkness, exactly when floods, fires and earthquakes need eyes on the ground, and NISAR maps nearly all of Earth’s land and ice twice every 12 days.
details:
Every 12 days, NISAR maps nearly all of Earth’s land and ice, through cloud, smoke and darkness. Petrova Line teaches anyone to read what it sees.

What it does
Petrova Line turns NISAR, the joint NASA–ISRO radar mission, into something you can explore with your own hands. It has two parts.

The story is a 3D scroll presentation. It opens on a planet wrapped in dozens of satellite orbits and finds NISAR on its 747 km sun-synchronous path. From there you:

  • fly in to its 12 m reflector;
  • follow its two radar waves to the ground (L-band 24 cm and S-band 9.4 cm, drawn at their true ratio);
  • watch 12 days of passes cover the planet;
  • visit four places that are changing: a retreating Caspian shore, the flooded Pantanal, the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquake and the Jakobshavn glacier.

The console is a full-screen radar map:

  • Compare dates: drag a divider between two dates.
  • Change the view: switch between HH, HV and VV polarisation, an InSAR interferogram and false colour, and between L-band and S-band.
  • Radar against camera: turn on a camera view with clouds and see what optical satellites miss.
  • Read a pixel: tap any pixel and the echo splits into surface, volume and double-bounce scattering, while the map lights up where each one dominates.
  • Ask “what if”: change the ground’s roughness and moisture and watch the signal respond.
  • Watch it change: a 2020–2026 timeline plays the change.
  • Take it away: a one-click brief exports the findings as Markdown, JSON or text.

How it works
Every pixel is described by its physical state on a given date: roughness, moisture, vegetation volume, vertical structure, coherence and ground motion. One backscatter model turns that state into what the radar would record at each polarisation and band. Because of that, the image, the pixel breakdown and the what-if sliders always agree.

Interferograms follow the real rule: one colour cycle for each half-wavelength of motion toward the satellite, which is 11.9 cm at L-band and 4.7 cm at S-band. The radar scenes are simulated from NISAR’s published parameters.

The globe is built from NASA’s 4K Blue Marble and Black Marble imagery, with terrain shading, cloud shadows and sun glint, and NISAR flies at its real altitude and inclination. Everything runs in the browser: no server, no login, and it works offline once installed.

Why it matters
Radar sees through cloud, smoke and darkness, exactly when floods, wildfires, earthquakes and storms need eyes on the ground. NISAR’s data is free and open. But a radar image is hard to read: it is grainy and grey, and its bright and dark areas don’t mean what our eyes expect.

Petrova Line is the on-ramp. In a few minutes, a student, a journalist or a flood planner can learn:

  • why a flooded forest glows bright;
  • why calm water turns black;
  • how a pattern of coloured fringes measures centimetres of ground movement.

Then they can open real NISAR data with confidence. The more people who can read radar, the more lives and livelihoods this free data can protect.

How it is creative
The challenge is about dancing with SARs, so we built the experience as a performance. The scroll conducts it and the camera moves with the satellite.

Instead of showing radar images as finished pictures, we let people take the physics apart one pixel at a time. And we put a cloud-covered camera view next to the radar view of the same place, so the case for radar makes itself.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: NISAR’s real orbit, wavelengths and fringe spacing, and a plain statement that the scenes are simulated.
  • Reach: it installs on phones, tablets and laptops, works offline and needs no account, which matters where the internet is slow or unreliable.
  • Performance: the 3D view lowers its resolution when needed to stay smooth on ordinary laptops, and heavy work runs off the main thread.
  • Accessibility: keyboard control, screen-reader labels, and a reduced-motion mode that turns camera flights into simple cuts.
  • Clarity: as few words as possible; numbers and motion tell the story.
  • Openness: NASA open data and no tracking.

Tools

  • Languages: TypeScript, plus GLSL for the custom WebGL shaders.
  • Libraries: React, Vite and Tailwind CSS for the app; Three.js for the 3D; GSAP and Lenis for motion and smooth scrolling; Motion and zustand.
  • Browser features: Web Workers for off-thread work, and a service worker for offline use.
  • Other tools: Playwright for testing and rendering, and Python (Pillow) to prepare the Earth maps.
  • AI: Petrova Line was designed, built and directed by our team. We researched and chose the concept, the four study sites, the story structure, the radar physics to explain factors (roughness, moisture, structure, phase) and how each scene is simulated from NISAR’s published parameters. We used AI coding assistants to speed up implementation and debugging. Every part was specified, reviewed, tested and adjusted by us. No AI-generated images or NASA branding are used.
  • Hardware: none beyond an ordinary computer; it is built to run on everyday laptops and phones.
